title: uTimerScript Usage
prompt: What is uTimerScript useful for in a mission, what kinds of variables should it post, and what are common mistakes when using it to initialize or trigger autonomy?

notebook.text:
uTimerScript is a MOOS application used to script a sequence of variable-value pairs (pokes) to the MOOSDB at specified times
1
2
. It is highly versatile, supporting randomization, logic conditions, and script flow control to automate mission events or simulate hardware
3
4
.
Usefulness in a Mission
Simulating Hardware: It can act as a proxy for sensors or external factors when they are unavailable. For example, it can simulate a GPS unit by posting heartbeats only when a vehicle is at the surface, including a random delay for satellite acquisition
5
6
. It can also simulate environmental effects like random wind gusts by posting drift vectors to uSimMarine
7
8
.
Automating Command and Control: It can mimic human interaction, such as automatically deploying a vehicle by posting DEPLOY=true and MOOS_MANUAL_OVERRIDE=false after a set time
9
.
Mission Scripting: It is used to generate data for other apps, such as a script that generates 100 random "visit points" for a path-planning algorithm
10
11
.
Dynamic Behavior Testing: It can cue the dynamic spawning of behaviors (e.g., collision avoidance) by posting variables that satisfy behavior "spawn" conditions
12
13
.
Kinds of Variables Posted
User-Configured Events: Any MOOS variable and value specified in the configuration block (e.g., DEPLOY, WIND_GUSTS, DRIFT_VECTOR_ADD)
14
15
.
Status Information (UTS_STATUS): It periodically publishes a summary string including elapsed time, number of events posted/pending, paused state, and number of resets
16
17
.
Exit Notification (EXITED_NORMALLY): If a script includes a quit event, it posts its own name to this variable upon completion so that monitoring tools like uProcessWatch can excuse its disappearance
17
18
.
Variable Types: Values are automatically posted as doubles if they are numerical and strings otherwise
14
. If a value consists solely of a macro (e.g., $[DBTIME]), it posts as a double
19
.
Common Mistakes and "Gotchas"
Timing and Handshaking Race Conditions: A script often starts its timer as soon as uTimerScript launches
20
21
. If it posts initialization variables before the receiving app (like the Helm) has fully connected or registered for those variables, the "poke" may be missed or ignored
22
. It is better to launch scripts in a paused mode and have a stable app un-pause them once the mission is ready
22
.
Variable Type Mismatch: Because MOOSDB enforces the type of a variable based on its first publication, if uTimerScript heuristically posts a value as a double (e.g., val=1) but the receiving app expects a string (e.g., "1"), the poke may fail or cause subsequent valid posts to be ignored
23
24
.
Logic Conditions on Virgin Variables: If a script is conditioned on a variable (e.g., condition = COUNTER_A > 5), the condition will evaluate to false if COUNTER_A has never been written to the MOOSDB, even if a "not-equal" logic like !=true is used
25
.
Triggering Spawns While Parked: If a script posts a variable intended to spawn a behavior, the spawn will not occur until the Helm has transitioned from PARK to the DRIVE state
26
.
Process Watcher False Alarms: Because uTimerScript is often designed to finish and quit, it will trigger a "process missing" warning in uProcessWatch unless it is explicitly "excused" via an EXITED_NORMALLY post or removed from the watch list
27
28
.
Burst Logging Failures: If a script posts a large burst of new variables (e.g., 100 random points), pLogger may miss them because it takes time to detect and register for new variables appearing in the MOOSDB
29
.

chatgpt.text:
uTimerScript is useful when you want a repeatable timed script of MOOS posts during a mission. It is basically an automated uPokeDB: at configured times, it posts variable-value pairs to the MOOSDB. The official MOOS-IvP docs describe it as an app that “script[s] a set of pre-configured posts to a MOOSDB,” often for initializing variables or replaying a timed sequence of mission events. 
oceanai.mit.edu

In a mission, use it for things like:

moos
ProcessConfig = uTimerScript
{
  AppTick   = 4
  CommsTick = 4

  paused     = false
  reset_max  = unlimited

  event = var=DEPLOY, val=true, time=5
  event = var=MOOS_MANUAL_OVERRIDE, val=false, time=5
  event = var=RETURN, val=false, time=5
}

The most common legitimate uses are:

Start/autonomy triggers
Post things like:

DEPLOY = true
MOOS_MANUAL_OVERRIDE = false
RETURN = false

This is similar to what the DEPLOY button in pMarineViewer or a uTermCommand shortcut often does: post MOOS_MANUAL_OVERRIDE=false and DEPLOY=true. 
oceanai.mit.edu

Initial mission state
Post simple flags your behaviors or apps expect:

MISSION_MODE = SURVEY
AVOID = true
STATION_KEEP = false
LOITER_UPDATES = ...
WPT_UPDATE = ...

Simulation-only scripted events
For testing, you can inject artificial events:

SWIMMER_ALERT = x=20,y=-40
SENSOR_CONTACT = name=alpha,x=50,y=10
TASK_ASSIGNMENT = id=3,type=rescue,x=...

Behavior updates at known times
It can post update strings to behaviors, for example changing waypoint points, loiter radius, speed, or conditions mid-mission.

The key rule: uTimerScript should post high-level mission variables, not low-level navigation truth.

Good variables to post:

DEPLOY
MOOS_MANUAL_OVERRIDE
RETURN
STATION_KEEP
MISSION_MODE
WPT_UPDATE
LOITER_UPDATE
SURVEY_UPDATE
OPREGION_UPDATE
TASK_REQUEST
NODE_MESSAGE_LOCAL

Bad or suspicious variables to post:

NAV_X
NAV_Y
NAV_HEADING
NAV_SPEED
DESIRED_HEADING
DESIRED_SPEED
IVPHELM_STATE
APPCAST
NODE_REPORT

Those should normally come from the nav source, simulator, helm, reporter, or relevant app. If you use uTimerScript to fake them, you may make the mission look alive while hiding the fact that the real pipeline is broken.

Common mistakes:

1. Using it as a crutch for broken launch/configuration

If the helm only works because uTimerScript posts DEPLOY=true, that is fine for simulation, but you should still know where the real operator/deploy path is. In many missions, deployment comes from pMarineViewer, uPokeDB, uTermCommand, or a launch script. uTimerScript should not be the only mysterious place where autonomy becomes active.

2. Posting DEPLOY=true but forgetting MOOS_MANUAL_OVERRIDE=false

A very common failure is:

DEPLOY = true

but the helm remains effectively parked because manual override is still true. Usually the deploy pair is:

DEPLOY = true
MOOS_MANUAL_OVERRIDE = false

3. Posting too early

If uTimerScript posts before pHelmIvP, your planner app, or your custom behavior has registered/subscribed, the post may still exist in the DB, but some apps may miss the mail event they expected. Safer pattern:

time=2: initialize mission flags
time=5: deploy
time=7: send behavior updates

For debugging, check the timestamps in uXMS or the .alog.

4. Confusing initialization with behavior activation

Posting a variable does not guarantee a behavior runs. The behavior still needs:

condition = DEPLOY == true
condition = RETURN != true
condition = MISSION_MODE == SURVEY

to evaluate correctly, and the helm must be running, not parked, not overridden, and receiving NAV_X, NAV_Y, NAV_SPEED, and NAV_HEADING.

5. Posting the wrong type or spelling

MOOS variables are stringly enough that this can bite you:

DEPLOY = TRUE
DEPLOY = true
DEPLOY = 1
Deploy = true

These may not be equivalent depending on how the consuming app parses them. Match the exact spelling and expected value used in the .bhv and app code.

6. Accidentally looping/reposting forever

If reset_max or repeat settings are wrong, uTimerScript may repeatedly post a trigger. That can cause behaviors to restart, updates to overwrite live app decisions, or debugging to become confusing because the DB keeps changing “by itself.”

7. Using it to initialize variables that should come from real systems

For simulation, posting fake sensor/task/contact variables can be useful. For real vehicle runs, be careful. uTimerScript should not replace real nav, safety, comms, or payload state unless you are deliberately testing a failure mode.

Best mental model:

uTimerScript = scripted mission pokes
pAntler      = launches processes
.moos file   = configures processes
.bhv file    = defines helm behaviors and conditions
pHelmIvP     = turns behavior state + nav into DESIRED_* commands

So, when autonomy does not trigger, ask:

Did uTimerScript launch?
Did it post the variable?
Did the variable have the right name/value/type?
Did the helm/behavior actually depend on that variable?
Was the helm already running and receiving NAV_*?
Was MOOS_MANUAL_OVERRIDE false?

For your missions, I would use uTimerScript mainly for repeatable simulation startup and event injection, not as the permanent source of truth for mission state.

Good, I have the full official docs. Here's a thorough breakdown:

uTimerScript in MOOS-IvP Missions
What it's useful for

uTimerScript lets you script a set of pre-configured posts to the MOOSDB. In its most basic form, it can initialize variables and immediately terminate itself if a quit event is included. More broadly, it covers three main use cases: 
Mit

1. Mission initialization / deploy trigger. The most common simple use: post the handful of variables needed to get the helm running, then quit. The following config, placed in a mission file, mimics pressing the DEPLOY button — disabling manual override, deploying the vehicle, and then quitting:

event = var=MOOS_MANUAL_OVERIDE, val=false
event = var=DEPLOY, val=true
event = quit

mit

2. Simulation proxy. uTimerScript may be used to effectively simulate the output of other MOOS applications when those applications aren't available — for example, a simulated GPS unit or a crude simulation of wind gusts. This avoids having to write and distribute a whole new MOOS app just to fake a sensor signal. 
mit

3. Timed/periodic event sequences. Each entry in the script happens after a specified elapsed time. Scripts may be paused or fast-forwarded, events may be configured with random values, and events can be scheduled to happen randomly within a chosen time window. 
Mit

What kinds of variables to post

The right variables depend on your mission, but there are canonical categories:

Helm control flags — these are the core autonomy triggers:

DEPLOY (true/false) — starts the helm executing behaviors
MOOS_MANUAL_OVERIDE (false) — hands control to the helm (note the original typo is in the MOOS variable name itself)
RETURN (true/false) — activates a return behavior
STATION_KEEP (true/false) — activates station-keeping

Simulated sensor heartbeats — when a real sensor isn't present in simulation. For example, GPS_UPDATE_RECEIVED can be posted as a proxy for the GPS heartbeat signal that the autonomy system uses to confirm that a surface excursion was successful, conditioned on NAV_DEPTH < 0.2 to simulate the vehicle being at the surface with a random acquisition delay of 20–120 seconds. 
mit

Environmental disturbance variables — for robustness testing. DRIFT_VECTOR_ADD can be posted in sequences to simulate wind gusts, using random-variable macros for angle and magnitude that are re-randomized on each script reset. 
mit

Application-specific variables — anything a behavior reads as a condition, like WIND_GUSTS, SBR_RANGE_REQUEST, or custom mission state flags.

Common mistakes when using it to initialize or trigger autonomy

1. Forgetting MOOS_MANUAL_OVERIDE = false. If you only post DEPLOY = true but leave manual override enabled, the helm won't actually take control. Both variables usually need to be set together.

2. Not including event = quit. Before quitting, a final posting to EXITED_NORMALLY is made so that watchdog processes like uProcessWatch know the exit is intentional and not a crash. If you want uTimerScript to act only as an initializer and then get out of the way, forgetting event = quit leaves it running unnecessarily. 
mit

3. Timing collisions — posting before the helm is ready. The block_on parameter causes the script to wait until specified MOOS apps appear in the list of DB_CLIENTS. Without this, a fast-starting uTimerScript can post DEPLOY = true before pHelmIvP has even connected, and the post gets lost. 
mit

4. Typos in string vs. double types. A value is posted as a double if it looks numerical, and as a string otherwise. If you want to post the string "99" rather than the double 99, you must add quotes around it. Similarly, a string value containing a comma (like "apples, pears") must be quoted or the comma will be misinterpreted as a field separator. 
mit

5. Condition logic never becoming true. If you use condition = DEPLOY = true to gate the script, but DEPLOY is never posted to the DB before the script checks, the script sits paused indefinitely. Make sure the variables your condition depends on are actually being published by the time uTimerScript starts checking.

6. Multiple uTimerScript instances stomping on each other. If multiple scripts are running in the same MOOS community, they all listen to UTS_PAUSE, UTS_RESET, and UTS_FORWARD by default. Posting to any of these will affect all running scripts unless each is configured with a unique pause_var, reset_var, and forward_var. 
mit

7. Not using upon_awake = restart for condition-gated loops. If you want a script to restart fresh every time conditions are re-met (e.g., every time the vehicle surfaces), you need upon_awake = restart. Without it, the script will just resume from where it left off rather than re-running from the beginning.

gemini.text:
In the MOOS-IvP autonomy framework, uTimerScript is a powerful, lightweight utility used to script a series of pre-configured posts (variable-value pairs) to the MOOSDB at specific times or under specific logical conditions.

Think of it as a scriptable puppet master for your simulation or mission, capable of mimicking human interaction, simulating external environments, or managing the initial lifecycle of your autonomous agent.

1. What is uTimerScript Useful For?

Initialization: Bootstrapping a mission by setting baseline variables in the MOOSDB immediately upon startup, then safely quitting (event = quit) so it doesn't consume background processing power.

Simulating the Environment: Emulating real-world unpredictability without needing complex environmental physics engines. For example, it can periodically post WIND_GUST variables or randomly change a stream of water currents (DRIFT_VECTOR).

Simulating Hardware/Sensors: Providing fake sensor streams when hardware isn't available. A classic textbook use case is simulating a GPS unit on a UUV (Unmanned Underwater Vehicle) that only posts GPS_UPDATE = true when the vehicle surfaces.  
MIT Marine Autonomy Lab

Automated Testing and Stress Testing: Rapidly feeding mock data (like spawning dynamic obstacle locations for collision avoidance testing) to see how the IvP Helm (pHelmIvP) responds.

2. What Kinds of Variables Should It Post?

uTimerScript can post both doubles and strings. Depending on what aspect of the mission you are targeting, it commonly posts:

Mission Lifecycle & State Variables

DEPLOY = true / DEPLOY = false (Triggers the main helm states)

MOOS_MANUAL_OVERRIDE = false (Hands control over to the autonomy helm)

MISSION_START = true

Sensor & Simulation Data

GPS_FIX = true or NAV_X = $(X) + sin($(TIME)) (Using macro expansions to generate mock movement or coordinates)

BATTERY_VOLTAGE = 11.4 (Simulating battery drain over time)

Operational Parameters / Updates

UP_LOITER = "center_activate=true" (Using the updates parameter in behaviors to dynamically change paths or behaviors mid-mission)

RETURN = true (Simulating an emergency low-battery return trigger)

3. Common Mistakes When Initializing or Triggering Autonomy

Because uTimerScript runs asynchronously and relies entirely on string/double matching, a few tiny syntax or architectural missteps can easily stall an entire mission.

Type Mismatching (Strings vs. Doubles)

MOOS variables lock onto the data type of the very first message published to them. uTimerScript guesses the type based on a heuristic: if it looks like a number, it posts a double; otherwise, it posts a string.  
MIT Marine Autonomy Lab

The Mistake: Writing event = var=DEPLOY, val=1 when your helm behavior expects condition = DEPLOY = true (a string).

The Consequence: The condition will silently evaluate to false forever because a double (1) cannot equal a string ("true"), even if they logically mean the same to you.

Tip: If you want a number handled as a string, wrap it in quotes: val="99".

Race Conditions with pHelmIvP (The "Premature Post")

If uTimerScript is set to paused = false (the default) and immediately posts DEPLOY = true at time = 0, it might post to the MOOSDB before pHelmIvP has fully booted up, initialized its logic buffers, and subscribed to the variable.

The Consequence: The trigger message is lost into the ether. When the helm finally finishes loading, it looks at the database, misses the event, and sits idle.

Fix: Always give your startup events a slight delay (e.g., time = 5.0) to let the rest of the MOOS community stabilize.

Misunderstanding Logic Conditions (condition vs. run_condition)

You can constrain a script using lines like condition = (NAV_SPEED > 1).

The Mistake: Expecting a script to instantly reset or fire the moment a condition becomes true. By default, when a script's conditions are unmet, it simply pauses its internal timer. When the conditions are met again, it resumes exactly where it left off.

Fix: If you want the script to completely wipe its progress and start from scratch every time a condition toggles back to true, you must explicitly set shuffle = true or utilize the reset_max and reset_var settings.

Case Sensitivity Pitfalls

MOOS variables are strictly case-sensitive, but logic evaluations inside configurations handle strings case-insensitively.

The Mistake: Writing event = var=deploy, val=true instead of var=DEPLOY.

The Consequence: You will create a brand new variable named deploy in lowercase, while your IvP Helm continues to wait for DEPLOY in uppercase.
